issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For physical abuse by a romantic partner, the threat profile is centered on generalized danger from strangers, while the appraisals are centered on bodily damage/shame and permanent emotional change. This is not impossible, but as the only represented components it is clinically hard to integrate into a single coherent profile of partner abuse without any partner-specific or trauma-linked threat content.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active links are between Negative Appraisals and Threat, so these two nodes should strongly cohere. Here the negative appraisals imply consequences focused on the body and self after intimate physical abuse, but the threat item 'threat from strangers approaching me' points to a different danger representation that is not reflected in the appraisals. That weakens the expected tight appraisal-threat coupling.

vignette: Aroha, an eighty-year-old Māori welder who has spent her life turning metal into tools for her community, has carried the invisible weight of a decades-old assault by the man she married. Their marriage began with promise, but on a July afternoon in the 1990s, the man-who had once been a promising carpenter-hit her in the shoulder while she was bent over a welding table, the metal sparks still flying from her torch. The blow left a bruise that never faded, a permanent reminder of the moment her body was no longer safe in his presence. Even after that day, he would return to the kitchen and press his fist into her arm in frustration, each strike leaving a fresh scar and a new sense of dread. In the weeks that followed, Aroha's nights became a battleground. The thought that her body might fail again made her sleep fragile; she could not fall or stay asleep. When the darkness settled, she would wake with the instinct to check the doors, the windows, the familiar rustling of the shop's ventilation system that now felt like an enemy. She would stand for long stretches, eyes wide, listening to the hiss of coolant and the hiss of her own breathing, convinced that if she didn't stay alert, the next blow could come at any moment. The belief that her body was permanently damaged-an image that had crystallized from that first hit-fed into this threat, so that the more she felt her body's unreliability, the more she stayed on guard. Her fear of injury was not just a residual echo; it was a living, breathing force that pulled her from sleep and into a constant state of readiness. That sleepless vigilance, in turn, hardened the very conviction that her body was beyond repair. Each night she stayed up, each moment of trembling awareness, reinforced the notion that she could never trust her own flesh again. The feeling of danger did not dissipate; instead, it seeped into her sense of self, convincing her that her capacity for normal emotion had been lost forever. The cycle of threat and appraisal grew tighter, each loop making her feel more isolated in her own home, despite the presence of her spouse, who now seemed to be a distant echo of the person who had once held her hand. The relentless cycle spilled over into her work. Aroha still walked into the welding shop on the edge of town every Thursday, where the bright glare of arc light and the clatter of metal would set her nerves alight. The hiss of the oxygen tank, the metallic scent of hot steel-these sensory cues triggered the same hypervigilance that kept her awake at night. She would pause before she could lift the torch, breathing heavily, the memory of the earlier blows flaring into her mind. Her fear of the shop's environment forced her to skip shifts, to hand over tasks to younger apprentices, and eventually, to retire from the shop entirely. This avoidance of the very place that had once been her livelihood further isolated her, amplifying her belief that she was no longer capable of functioning safely. Now, at eighty, Aroha finds herself in a quiet room at the community health center, her heart racing as she speaks. She tells the therapist that she has lost the simple joys of her life: the quiet comfort of sleep, the sense of trust in her own body, and the ability to feel normal emotions. She is terrified that the cycle of threat and negative appraisal will never break. Yet, she also holds a fragile hope-that with time and help, she might learn to let go of the constant guard, to trust the metal beneath her hands and the silence of her own bedroom. Her present fear is not just of physical harm; it is the dread that she will never again feel safe enough to let herself rest, to let herself be vulnerable, and to let herself love again.
